data.title: Bertelsmann rules out gaming push despite GTA VI frenzy, CEO says
data.description: Nov 19 : Bertelsmann has no plan to enter the video games market despite the blockbuster success of "Grand Theft Auto VI," said Thomas Rabe, CEO of the German media group that published the original game in the franchise. Huge global demand for GTA VI is expected to generate revenue far exceeding its estimated development costs of around $1 billion. But "not every game becomes as successful as GTA," Rabe said and cautioned that gaming remains a hit-driven business, similar to the film industry. "New games are not easy to establish." Bertelsmann's BMG Interactive division published the first "Grand Theft Auto" in 1997. The next year, the company sold the business to Take-Two Interactive, which went on to develop one of the world's most successful gaming franchises. Rabe said his company has repeatedly examined entering the gaming market over the past 10 to 15 years, but decided against it. He cited high acquisition costs, reputational risks and the industry's reliance on a few blockbusters. Bertelsmann, whose businesses include broadcaster RTL Group, publisher Penguin Random House, music company BMG and logistics provider Arvato, sees little need to expand into other sectors, Rabe said.

data.title: Astronomers observe a huge puffy star merge with smaller companion
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Astronomers have observed a large dying star, seven times more massive and 18,000 times brighter than the sun, engulfing a smaller companion in a stellar merger unlike any other previously witnessed. The merger involved a pair of stars that were bound gravitationally — known as a binary system — in which the larger one greatly expanded in its death throes into what is called a puffy supergiant and enveloped the smaller one, with the two stars then combining into one. This cosmic connection occurred about 2.5 million light-years from Earth on the outskirts of the Andromeda Galaxy, one of our Milky Way's closest galactic neighbors. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km). The researchers identified the impending engulfment nearly three years before it occurred and then watched as the merger unfolded, step by step. "Giant stars engulfing their companion stars have been theorized for many decades, and understanding the outcomes of this process has important implications for explaining a wide range of systems that we see today in the universe," said Viraj Karambelkar, a postdoctoral researcher and NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York, lead author of the research published in the journal Nature. "The system presented in this study provides the first direct observations of this process happening — the first time a giant star engulfing its companion was caught in the act," Karambelkar said. Large stars near the end of their lifespan can swell up as their cores run out of fuel and shrink while the inner stellar heat pushes the outer layers outward. The larger star in this study puffed up to 350 times the sun's diameter. The smaller star, whose diameter was about 70 per cent that of the sun, orbited its companion at roughly the same distance as between Mars and the sun, and was engulfed in the bigger star's expansion. 'SET OFF A BOMB' The researchers detected brightening when this occurred in 2018, and the smaller star began to spiral inward toward the core of the bigger star over the next seven years. Toward the end of 2025, the smaller star finally merged with the core of the larger one, triggering an eruption a million times brighter than the sun in what Karambelkar called "a unification event." "This violent collision set off a bomb inside the star, producing the bright eruption that we saw," Karambelkar said. The researchers first spotted the stars using data from the infrared WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California and NASA's NEOWISE space telescope, then watched the events with the orbiting SPHEREx and James Webb space telescopes and various ground-based observatories. "We have observed mergers of stars in the past," said Columbia astrophysics professor and study co-author Kishalay De. "The difference is in the nature of the stars that merged. In the past, stellar mergers were observed from two stars that were fairly small and compact, and their merger was almost inevitable once they came into physical contact. However, the bigger star in this event was a very puffed-up star where its outer envelope was loosely bound. This configuration is exactly the kind in which a merger may or may not happen," De said. In some cases, an engulfed smaller star might release enough energy to blow away the larger star's puffy outer layers, leaving behind the remaining core of the original bigger star orbiting the smaller one, De said. While the larger of the two stars in this instance was nearing the end of its life, the merger may have produced a rejuvenated star with a new lease on life, the researchers said. The researchers gave the merged star the nickname Bao, the name of popular steamed buns in Chinese cuisine. "The auto-assigned name to this eruption was AT2025abao — 'Astronomical Transient in 2025 abao.' We called it Bao as an affectionate term derived from this. The similarity with the Chinese buns definitely encouraged us to adopt the nickname," Karambelkar said.

data.title: Thailand must keep US as major trade partner, PM says
data.description: BANGKOK, Nov 20 : Thailand must keep the United States as a major trade partner and cannot lose it to its competitors, its Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Friday, as his government defended a trade deal with Washington. • Thailand and the United States this week signed a joint statement about a "substantial conclusion" to negotiations on reciprocal trade • Opening Thailand's market to more US goods does not require government purchases, but would give private importers another source for products, Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun told a briefing • Thailand is in talks with Washington to cut a US tariff to 10 per cent from 12.5 per cent, she said • The country should not face less favourable terms than neighbouring countries that have signed reciprocal trade agreements with the US, as a widening tariff gap could hurt exports and employment, she said • The US is Thailand's largest export market, with exports worth about 2.37 trillion baht ($69.81 billion) in 2025 and linked to around 1.25 million jobs, the commerce ministry said • The joint statement is not the final agreement, with a legal review, a signing and some domestic procedures still to be completed before it takes effect, Suphajee said • Thailand will not allow imports of US pork containing ractopamine, the commerce ministry said ($1 = 33.95 baht)

data.title: Chile, Japan to boost cooperation on critical minerals, Chile's Kast says
data.description: SANTIAGO, Nov 20 : Chile will seek to strengthen cooperation with Japan on critical minerals to ensure resilience and stability in supply chains, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said on Friday. • "We are committed to strengthening cooperation on critical minerals, including copper," Kast said after meeting Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during an official visit to Japan • Chile is the world's largest copper producer and second-largest lithium producer. Both metals are key to electric vehicles and battery energy storage systems • The cooperation will "contribute to the resilience and stability of global supply chains by ensuring that trade measures are consistent with relevant international agreements", a joint statement added • Kast and Takaichi cited a project at Chilean state-run Codelco's El Teniente copper mine as a concrete example of their cooperation • In August, the mine began testing a next-generation photonics communication network developed in Japan • They also backed a free international economic order and signed a memorandum of cooperation on information and communication technologies

data.title: Big Pharma, with eye on Anthropic, says AI is shrinking drug discovery timelines
data.description: NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 20 : Artificial intelligence has sped up early-stage drug development work at some of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies this year, cutting by as much as half the time it takes to produce new molecules and move them into the clinic, according to their top scientists. GSK, Bristol Myers Squibb, Novartis, Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, AstraZeneca and Sanofi all say they have moved beyond less glamorous tasks for AI like preparing regulatory filings. They are now using the technology for designing molecules, sorting out the most promising ones, and identifying safety risks. “There is no part of the discovery through development pipeline where we are not using AI,” AstraZeneca executive Sharon Barr said. Some of the scientists say decades of drug discovery experience and data give them an advantage over AI companies like Anthropic, which is gearing up to be a rival, partner or both, with a $1.5 trillion initial public offering this week. In recent months, it opened its own laboratory and announced other investments, part of pushing AI to speed drug discovery. On Thursday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, at the Nasdaq before shares began trading, spoke of his father dying of a disease shortly before a cure was found. Although clinical trials and experiments will still take time, he said, "I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future, fewer families miss a cure by a few years." Drug companies are gauging whether the upstart can succeed in tackling disease. Historically, nearly 9 out of 10 drugs developed using conventional methods fail in clinical trials. It can cost billions of dollars and take 10 to 15 years to bring a drug to market, according to industry lobby group PhRMA. Aliza Apple, who runs Lilly's TuneLab, which gives smaller biotechs access to some of the drugmaker's internal AI models to promote collaboration, said claims like those made by Amodei and the founders of Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs that the technology is capable of curing all disease overstate current capabilities. “It would be great for them to cure one, and then let's talk about the rest,” she said. CONCRETE RESULTS Pharma company scientists say their AI programs are already yielding concrete results. Sanofi said it saved at least a year developing asthma treatment lunsekimig using an AI-enabled approach to translate early biology into clinical decisions that let the company skip a dose-selection study. Novartis said AI tools helped it find five targets it prioritized for developing kidney disease treatments. Bristol Myers said one of its sickle cell anemia candidates would not have been developed without the company's AI systems. It's using AI to refine new molecules and run simulations based on its trial data to determine which ones should progress, Chief Research Officer Robert Plenge said. "The next area for us is to tie those models into laboratory automation... to make better, high-quality molecules faster,” he added. Novo Nordisk said AI has cut the number of cycles of designing, manufacturing and testing new molecules from around eight to three and slashed the time of each cycle from eight weeks to four. Still, the number of AI-enabled drugs in clinical testing has only climbed incrementally. In March, researchers identified 129 drug candidates across 69 companies, up from around 117 eight months earlier. Most of the programs remain in early-stage development. “I think over the next 1, 2, 3 years we'll see a sharp uptick in AI drugs being developed pre-clinically and also drugs that go to clinical trials,” said Dr. Waqas Haque, an oncology fellow at University of Chicago who was on the team that compiled the data. “I don't know if those drugs are going to be more successful than non-AI drugs, and I don't think they're going to be approved any quicker,” he said, because of bottlenecks with human trials and regulators. 'JUST THE BEGINNING' Anthropic's Amodei has long said curing disease is one of the main benefits AI can provide to humanity. The company is working on its own and with partners like Bristol Myers to develop new drugs. It launched scientific research-focused AI software called Claude Science, and added Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan to its board. Other companies, including Novo Nordisk, use Anthropic models and Claude Science in their R&D work. Luca Giani, senior principal at venture capital firm Alumni Ventures, said Anthropic — and rival frontier labs — are shopping for pharma-related acquisitions. "They are out to get more data, and they are out to get more of the companies," Giani said. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment on its acquisition plans and the nature of its relationship with drugmakers. Even before its $1.5 trillion IPO, Anthropic announced several partnerships and an acquisition last month, he said. "I think it's just the beginning." Lilly’s Apple said Anthropic and AI rivals can be viewed as allies and competitors. “In the early days, we certainly saw them as vendors. To be fair, that's how they framed themselves. I think we increasingly see them as collaborators,” Apple said. “A year ago they weren't doing any programs, and a year from now, it's anyone's guess.” GSK Chief Scientific Officer Tony Wood said he views Anthropic “as another competitor,” while Bristol Myers and Novo see the AI companies more as partners. Still, Novo said it does not provide proprietary data to frontier labs to train their AI models, nor does Sanofi. “If you don’t have the data to train the model on, then it breaks down very quickly,” said Matt Truppo, global head of computational & AI strategy for Sanofi R&D. Truppo said he expects AI to cut early-discovery timelines by 20 per cent to 25 per cent within two years, and perhaps by half within five years, across more than 100 drug development programs. It may be some time before this can be expanded beyond treatment areas where the company has the most proprietary data, he added. Novartis President of Biomedical Research Fiona Marshall said the average time from project start to a drug candidate has gone from three years to about 18 months to two years. “We have had a lot of data," Marshall said, "and now we can really use that data in a much more sophisticated way.”

data.title: Saudi Arabia once banned Grand Theft Auto. Now it's got a stake in it
data.description: Nov 20 : Grand Theft Auto, banned in Saudi Arabia until last year, is now being embraced not only by its gamers - a category that includes Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman - but also by its sovereign wealth fund, which the prince chairs. This week, gamers in Saudi Arabia joined legions of fans around the world to play Grand Theft Auto VI upon launch — the first new release of the top-selling series since a Saudi ban was scrapped in 2025. "Playing GTA VI in Saudi Arabia legally makes me so happy, because we're talking about a game that was banned," local content creator Thamer al Dairem said from a windowless, air-conditioned room, lit mostly by the bank of monitors displaying the game. "We're talking about the biggest game in the world." Support and investment in gaming by Saudi Arabia have been rising fast, not least from de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman, often known by his initials MBS, who told Fox News in 2023 that gaming helped him disconnect and let off steam. The Public Investment Fund (PIF), the sovereign wealth fund he chairs, owns a major stake worth over $2 billion in Take-Two Interactive, the US firm that owns Grand Theft Auto-developer Rockstar Games, LSEG Workspace data show. CHANGING CUSTOMS IN CONSERVATIVE SAUDI ARABIA In August, a consortium including PIF acquired gaming giant Electronic Arts for $55 billion. This month, gaming software provider Unity Software held talks with investors including the Saudi sovereign wealth fund on a potential buyout valuing it at around $25 billion. PIF, which has spent the past year consolidating its gaming holdings into a subsidiary, Savvy Games Group, declined to comment. MBS has been leading a campaign to open Saudi Arabia up and ease strict social and cultural norms that revolve around a conservative interpretation of Islam — a far cry from GTA VI's Vice City. GTA VI advertisements have been appearing in some of Saudi Arabia's most popular shopping malls. One image shows the heroine wearing shorts and a crop top, her arm resting on her partner's shoulder — unthinkable a few years ago, when women were required to dress modestly and cover their hair. MBS's wider reform plan, dubbed Vision 2030, is all about reducing reliance on oil and gas revenues, both in the economy and in state revenues, and PIF strategy is part of that. "(It) is part of a diversified long-term investment strategy to capture value from industries it does not traditionally operate within," said Piers Harding-Rolls, who researches games at Ampere Analysis. In Riyadh, al Dairem is now streaming Grand Theft Auto content and says that, while some of the depictions of violence, drugs and sex are extreme, the game is age-restricted and reflects another country. "The city is Vice City, and it's representing Miami and the chaotic things that happen. For us Saudis, like, we know that it has nothing to do with us." The gaming experience, on the other hand, matters hugely to him. "When I saw the ads of GTA VI in the malls, I was so happy. If you'd asked me if I was ever going to see this, like, 10 years ago in Saudi, I wouldn't have believed it." (Editing by Adam Jourdan and Kevin Liffey)

data.title: PayPal taps Xero's Claire Bramley as CFO, succeeding Jamie Miller
data.description: Nov 20 : PayPal named Xero's Claire Bramley as chief financial officer on Friday, succeeding Jamie Miller, in a broader shake-up of its senior leadership team as the payments firm pursues an ambitious turnaround. Once a pandemic-era darling, PayPal has lost ground as consumers increasingly turn to payment services embedded in their smartphones, leaving its shares well below the record highs reached in 2021. The shift has been amplified by the expansion of Big Tech into digital payments through services such as Google Pay and Apple Pay, chipping away at PayPal's market share and dampening investor confidence. Bramley is set to join PayPal on February 1 from Xero, a global small-business platform, where she has served as CFO since April 2025. In her new role, she will be tasked with advancing the company's multi-year plan to streamline operations, cut costs and improve margins as it seeks to stem market share losses and revive its stock price. PayPal has set a goal of securing at least $1.5 billion in gross run-rate savings over the next two to three years. The appointment is part of a wider management reshuffle at the company, which has also tapped American Express' Kartik Mani as president and head of consumer financial services and Venmo — a peer-to-peer payments platform. Juan Rio is set to join PayPal from Brightstar.AI as executive vice-president of AI business transformation and operations at the end of the month. Accelerating AI adoption through the integration of AI and automation across its business is crucial for its cost-cutting plan, accounting for about 40 per cent of the total savings target. In the most recent quarter, PayPal CEO Enrique Lores expressed growing confidence in its turnaround plan, as the company raised annual profit forecast. PayPal has a market value of about $47 billion, down sharply from its peak of roughly $360 billion in July 2021.

data.title: SK Hynix to become top shareholder in rival Kioxia after bond conversion
data.description: SEOUL, Nov 20 : South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix Inc will become the largest shareholder in Japanese rival Kioxia Holdings by converting bonds of an investment vehicle into shares in December. SK Hynix said it would convert the bonds into 129,000 common shares and buy 1,001 additional shares in the entity from Bain Capital, a transaction that will give SK Hynix an indirect stake of about 14.1 per cent in Kioxia. SK Hynix also said it had no current plans to buy or sell additional Kioxia shares and its participation in Kioxia's management would remain limited after the deal. The plan comes amid robust demand for NAND chips, used for storage in devices ranging from smartphones to servers in AI data centers. SK Hynix is the No.2 maker of NAND chips, with a 19 per cent share, while Kioxia ranks fourth with a 14 per cent share, according to research firm Counterpoint. In 2018, SK Hynix invested a total of 395 billion yen ($2.48 billion) in the Bain Capital-led consortium that acquired Toshiba Memory, now Kioxia. A Bain-managed investment vehicle completed the sale of all of its Kioxia shares in June, after Kioxia listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2024. ($1 = 159.0900 yen)

data.title: Anthropic's post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
data.description: Nov 20 : Anthropic's post-listing slide deepened the gloom over the AI sector on Friday, underscoring how even one of the most eagerly anticipated listings in history has struggled to revive investor enthusiasm. Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic's listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain momentum after a turbulent stretch. But the stock was last trading at $88.87, about 9 per cent below where it closed following Thursday's smooth debut, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about $1.6 trillion and a market capitalization of $1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding. The stock could find support later in the year. London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 per cent of Anthropic's shares by year-end. Near-term volatility, however, could persist as the initial euphoria around the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained. "We favor patience on Anthropic and recommend evaluating the company as it reports public results," said Kaush Amin, head of private market investing at US Bank Asset Management, adding that the current valuation "assumes years of rapid growth." The debut has also done little to ease broader concerns about the health of the AI trade. Wall Street's main indexes ended sharply lower on Thursday, while futures pointed to further declines on Friday. Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia and Meta Platforms fell more than 2 per cent each in premarket trading, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped more than 1 per cent. Chip stocks also slid, with AMD and Sandisk down 7 per cent each and Intel losing more than 5 per cent. The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which would be another major test of investors' appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public next year. PARALLELS WITH SPACEX Anthropic's IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record. While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX's sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing. "There's going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don't think there's any need to get on it on the first trade," said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co. SpaceX shares fell about 5 per cent. Retail investors traded about $772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012. The stock's sharp swings have left investors weighing whether to bet on a rebound or brace for further losses. Options trading, due to begin next week, could add to the volatility. "It's not a good environment for Anthropic at the moment," said Carsten Hesse, head of index events at Berenberg. Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment. Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, Bloomberg News reported on Friday.

data.title: ECB's Lagarde: cyber threat boosted by AI is my top worry
data.description: FRANKFURT, Nov 20 : The greatest immediate challenge facing the world of finance may be cyber threats supercharged by increasingly sophisticated AI agents, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Friday. Attackers are often anonymous, and difficult to track, and rely on dubious funding often from "toxic states" that have a vested interest in disrupting the world, Lagarde said. "The one (worry) that keeps me awake, and many of you awake as well ... is AI applied together with cyber threat," Lagarde told the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, adding that policymakers have not paid enough attention to this threat.

data.title: Anthropic IPO haul rises to $93.5 billion after underwriters exercise greenshoe
data.description: Nov 20 : Anthropic said on Friday that its underwriters had exercised the "greenshoe" option to purchase additional shares, increasing ​the total proceeds from its initial public offering to roughly $93.5 billion.

data.title: PayPal names Claire Bramley as chief financial officer
data.description: Nov 20 : Payments firm PayPal said on Friday it has named Claire Bramley as chief financial officer, succeeding Jamie Miller, as part of a broader shake-up of its senior leadership team. The executive overhaul comes as PayPal pursues an aggressive turnaround plan to restore investor confidence, battered by intensifying competition from Apple, Google and newer fintech rivals. Bramley joins PayPal from Xero, a global small-business platform, where she has served as CFO since April 2025. Among other appointments, the company named American Express' Kartik Mani as president and head of consumer financial services and Venmo. Juan Rio is set to join PayPal from Brightstar.AI as executive vice-president of AI business transformation and operations at the end of the month.

data.title: Alphabet raises $4.19 billion in Canadian bond offering
data.description: Nov 20 : Alphabet has raised C$6 billion ($4.19 billion) through a four-tranche Canadian bond offering, according to a pricing term sheet filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday. Big technology companies are increasingly tapping debt markets and ​raising equity ⁠to bolster AI infrastructure, marking a shift from their traditional reliance on cash to fund investments. The money raised would be used for general corporate purposes, which could include repayment of outstanding debt, the Google parent said in the filing. Alphabet expects to receive about C$5.97 billion after underwriting discounts, or bank fees, and before expenses. The offering was priced on November 19 and is scheduled to settle on November 24. The notes are senior unsecured debt and have received a rating of Aa2 with a "stable" outlook from Moody's, and AA+ with a "stable" outlook from S&P, the filing showed. RBC Dominion Securities, Scotia Capital and TD Securities are joint book-running managers for the transaction, while CIBC World Markets is a co-manager. Big Tech rival Meta in October announced plans for its largest-ever equity offerings of around $97.5 billion, including stock sales of about $37.5 billion, and plans to later raise up to $60 billion through an at-the-market share-sale program, or a plan to sell shares into the market over time at prevailing prices. Alphabet had increased its equity offerings to $84.75 billion in June. Last month, the company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, versus analysts' expectation that it would come close to breaking even. ($1 = 1.4322 Canadian dollars)

data.title: Dollar set for fourth weekly gain, supported by Fed tightening expectations, AI-driven haven bid
data.description: LONDON, Nov 20 : The dollar was steady on Friday and was on track to rise for the fourth straight week as expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening underpinned the US currency and jitters over the AI trade sent investors fleeing to safe-haven assets. The dollar index was perched near the 103.9 level, around its strongest since early April 2025. The weeks-long rally accelerated on November 10, when hotter-than-expected US inflation data reinforced bets that the Federal Reserve would tighten policy and Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point hike in December should be considered.  The dollar was also supported by a reduced appetite for risk, with a multitude of AI-related concerns weighing on global stocks. Anthropic's record market debut on Thursday did little to revive investor confidence. MSCI's world index of stocks fell for a seventh straight session on Friday, the longest losing streak since 2023. Chris Turner, global head of markets at ING, said that while there is only a weak case for another steep correction in equities, "there is no reason for the Fed to drop its hawkish rhetoric anytime soon."  He pointed to next week's US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, a key inflation gauge for the Fed, which Turner said will likely confirm that the Fed needs to act. "For FX, that means a continued strong dollar and continued pressure on popular carry trades," he said. In FX carry trades, investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the Japanese yen and Swiss franc, to fund purchases of higher-yielding assets elsewhere, often in emerging markets. Adding to the hawkish-leaning narrative, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, while Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said the evidence did not suggest inflation was heading back to 2 per cent on its own. "The debate now is not really about whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December, but how much it will raise rates by," Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said.  "We still think 25 basis points is more likely," Kong added. "If they really want to quicken the pace of tightening, I think they will prefer to increase rates by 25 bps in consecutive meetings rather than deliver a bigger-than-usual hike."  Sterling languished near a one-year low against the dollar at $1.3105, and the euro struggled near its lowest level since April 2025 and last bought $1.0961.  YEN FIRMS ON INFLATION DATA The yen firmed 0.6 per cent against the dollar to 158.78 and is set to close the week with a small gain after three weeks of losses that had dragged the currency to near the key 160 level. Japan's annual core inflation accelerated to 2.2 per cent in October, staying above the central bank's 2 per cent target for a second straight month and pointing to broadening price pressures that strengthen the case for a near-term rate hike by the Bank of Japan. Analysts at Capital Economics argue the yen's recent weakness is unlikely to last. With long-term inflation expectations now around target, further increases in yields would be mostly in real terms, which, combined with their view that US yields will fall, should prove yen-positive, the analysts said.  ING's Turner also noted that a carry trade unwind should be a slight positive for the yen.

data.title: Exclusive-Signal restricts screenshots to block AI agents from reading messages
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 20 : Encrypted messaging service Signal said on Friday it would restrict screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats on phones, warning that the tech industry's push to embed AI in consumer devices was eroding its ability to guarantee privacy. Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. The move reflects growing tension between privacy-focused apps and the biggest tech companies, which are racing to roll out AI agents designed to see what is on a user's screen and take actions based on it. Signal identified as particularly worrisome the AI capabilities built directly into operating systems, like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence, because of how deeply they are integrated into people's devices. Operating systems maintain the environment in which Signal and other applications must exist, the company said. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post provided to Reuters ahead of its release on Signal's website. To prevent agents from scanning Signal messages, the service is introducing new settings blocking screenshot access on people's phones and switching those restrictions on by default. Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.      GETTING AROUND PROTECTIONS Agents that can take actions on behalf of users are billed as the next big wave of AI technology, capable of surfacing relevant information from across different apps and executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases autonomously, without direct instructions. However, that reach can get around the protections that apps like Signal build for themselves. Reuters reported earlier this week that Meta's Muse agent was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to access Signal messages on both an Apple computer and a phone using Google's Android system. In both cases, Muse used broad operating system-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull in the messages, using those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate. On Apple's macOS, for instance, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers for people with disabilities to navigate over to Signal, take screenshots of chats there, extract text from those pictures and reproduce the messages inside the Muse app. An operating system update from Apple this week effectively closed that specific pathway, but also introduced a new set of permissions aimed at agents that offers similar capabilities paired with additional user warnings. Meta said in response to Reuters' reporting that agents need to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and that Muse can access other apps only via permissions users explicitly grant. Signal said that developers should have straightforward ways of opting their apps out of such data processing by AI assistants entirely, specifically mentioning screen reading, notifications and other file system access. The service, owned by a non-profit foundation, promises its users a secure messaging experience by limiting the data it stores on its own servers, eschewing ads and offering end-to-end encryption, meaning it cannot access and read the conversations conducted on its app. AI systems that scan people's screens can undermine those protections by pulling the messages out of Signal's secure environment and into whatever other servers the agent is using, it said in the post.
